client: I've been feeling really on edge since my partner moved in last month. I keep worrying that we won't be able to adjust to living together, and I find myself overanalyzing every little disagreement. Part of me wonders if talking about it will help, because these anxious thoughts just keep circling in my head no matter what I do.
therapist: It sounds like this transition has been bringing up a lot of anxious thoughts for you, especially around how you and your partner navigate disagreements. When those worries start circling, have you noticed any patterns in what tends to trigger them the most?

client:
I think the biggest trigger is when my partner gets quiet during arguments. The silence makes me spiral because I immediately assume they're shutting me out or planning to leave. It's like my brain jumps to worst-case scenarios even when we're just having a normal disagreement. 

I've tried telling myself it's just their way of processing, but the anxiety still creeps in every time. It feels impossible to stay rational in those moments.
therapist: I hear how distressing those moments of silence feel for you—it's understandable that your mind would jump to those worried thoughts when things feel uncertain. What would it be like to explore some concrete ways to ground yourself when you notice that spiral starting?

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not sure grounding techniques would really help in those moments. When the silence hits and my mind starts racing, it feels like everything is falling apart—how can focusing on my breath or surroundings make that any better? It just seems too simple for how overwhelming the anxiety feels.
therapist: I can hear how deep that sense of overwhelm runs—when the anxiety feels that intense, simple strategies might understandably seem inadequate. Would you be open to exploring what happens if we pair grounding with naming those worst-case scenarios aloud, to shrink their power in the moment?

client:
I don't know... naming the worst-case scenarios out loud sounds terrifying. What if saying them makes them feel more real? I already get stuck in these anxious thought loops where I can't stop imagining everything going wrong. 

But I guess part of me is curious if saying them to someone else might make them seem less scary. It's just hard to trust that process when my brain keeps screaming that these fears are valid.
therapist: It makes complete sense that giving voice to those fears feels risky—like you're handing them more power. But I notice a glimmer of curiosity there too about whether sharing could soften their grip. What if we started small, with just one scenario that feels slightly less charged to name together?

client: I guess I can see what you're saying about starting small, but even that feels overwhelming. What if I share something and it just makes me feel worse? I’ve tried talking about things before, and sometimes it feels like it just amplifies the anxiety instead of helping. I’m not sure if I’m ready to trust that this will actually soften anything—it feels like opening a door I might not be able to close.
therapist: It sounds like you've had experiences where opening up actually intensified the anxiety instead of relieving it—that would make anyone hesitant to try again. I wonder if we could work at your pace, only exploring what feels manageable, with the option to pause anytime it feels too much?

client: Yeah, that's exactly how it feels—like opening up just makes everything worse sometimes. I want to trust the process, but part of me worries that even "going at my pace" might accidentally push me into that overwhelmed space again. How do we know when it's safe to keep talking versus when it's just retraumatizing me?
therapist: I hear that deep concern about being pushed past your limits—it's so important to honor that protective part of you that's saying "not too fast." What if we treated this like building a safety net together, where you always have control over the brakes? For example, could we agree on a clear signal for when you need to shift topics or take a pause?

client: I like the idea of having control over the brakes, but I'm worried I won't actually use the signal when I need to. Part of me feels like I should just push through the discomfort, even though that's what gets me overwhelmed. It's hard to trust myself to speak up when I'm feeling too anxious.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real tension between wanting to protect yourself and feeling like you "should" push through—that self-doubt about speaking up must make this feel even harder. What if we practiced using that signal right now, in this safe space, so you can experience how it feels to honor your limits without judgment?

client: I get what you're saying, but practicing here feels... fake, you know? Like in real life, people actually react badly when I set boundaries. My friend just last week got all huffy when I said I couldn't help her move apartments. It's not the same when it's just role-playing.
therapist: It makes sense that role-playing might feel artificial when you've had real experiences of people reacting poorly to your boundaries—that frustration and resignation come through clearly. What if we explore what made that moment with your friend so charged, to understand what's at stake when you consider speaking up?

client: I guess what made it so charged was that I really needed space that day, but when I tried to say no to hanging out, my friend got all quiet and distant. It felt like I was being punished for setting a boundary, and now I'm scared to speak up again because I don't want to lose people. But at the same time, I'm exhausted from always saying yes when I don't mean it.
therapist: It sounds like that moment with your friend tapped into a deep fear—that setting boundaries might cost you the connection you value. That exhaustion from constantly saying "yes" must feel heavy to carry. What do you think might happen if we explored small ways to assert your needs while also reassuring yourself that your worth isn't tied to others' reactions?

client:
I get what you're saying, but every time I try to say no to people, I immediately feel guilty afterward. Like I'm being selfish or letting them down. Even the idea of small boundaries makes me anxious—what if they get upset and stop wanting to be around me? 

I know logically that my worth shouldn't depend on others, but it's hard to actually believe that when I'm in the moment. The fear feels so real.
therapist: That guilt and fear of rejection sound so immediate and convincing when you're in those moments—it makes complete sense that logic gets drowned out. What if we looked at one recent "yes" you wish you'd said "no" to, and explored what that cost you versus what it might have cost to set the boundary?
